newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - UK inflation to stick above 3.0 pct in 96.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - UK inflation to stick above 3.0 pct in 96.

text.p: Underlying inflation in Britain will stay stubbornly above 3.0 percent this year, and is likely to prompt further interest rate rises before the general election due by May, UK economists said on Friday.
Economists estimate underlying inflation for the end of 1997 will be around 3.2 percent, on the back of stronger than expected UK inflation data released on Thursday.
"It's either going to stay at 3.3 or go to 3.4 percent in November, but it's not going to go down," said John O' Sullivan, economist at Natwest Markets.

Thursday's figures saw underlying inflation, a measure that excludes mortgage interest payments, rising to 3.3 percent year-on-year from 2.9 percent in September, putting the government's inflation target of 2.5 percent or below in jeopardy.

It was the highest inflation figure since September 1993, and combined with the sharp decline in unemployment figures released on Wednesday, is expected to put pressure on Chancellor of the Exchequer, Kenneth Clarke to raise interest rates further.
Clarke will have his monthly meeting with Bank of England governor, Eddie George on December 11.

"We've got a forecast for base rates of 7.25 percent at the end of next year," said Ian Stewart, UK economist at Merrill Lynch. Interest rates now stand at 6.0 percent after Clarke announced a shock quarter of a point rise on October 30.

"Given the projections in last week's Inflation Report and the news that RPIX (underlying) inflation rose to 3.3 percent in October, we expect the Bank to press for a further 1/4 percent rise at the 11 December meeting," Philip Shaw, Union Discount chief economist said.
The Bank of England last week suggested underlying inflation could rise above three percent year-on-year over the next few months.

Clarke insisted there was no cause for concern, saying the jump in inflation was to be expected due to unusually low inflation figures in October last year, and it would fall back within its target range over the next few months.

Ciaran Barr, UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, agreed the rise to 3.3 percent was overstated due to last year's good performance and saw inflation falling slightly towards the end of 1996 as sterling appreciation hit goods inflation.
Headline inflation (which includes mortgage interest payments) rose to 2.7 percent from 2.1 in September and is expected to rise still further into next year.
March short sterling futures were up two basis points to 93.25 at 0808 GMT on Friday, reflecting fears of rates being pushed up over seven percent early next year.
